As summer wore on, plague, crowned with the sun’s powerful rays, sent its arrows across the earth, never missing its targets. Nations bowed their heads beneath them and died. The grain that had grown so abundantly lay rotting on the ground in autumn. The miserable man who had gone out to gather food for his children lay cold in a furrow, killed by plague. Green woods swayed majestically, while dying people lay beneath their shade, answering the solemn music of the branches with harsh cries. Brightly colored birds darted among the shadows. Untroubled deer rested safely on the ferns. Oxen and horses wandered from their unattended stables and grazed in the wheat, for death struck human beings alone.

Our fears grew with the summer and the rising deaths. My poor beloved and I looked at each other and at our children. “We will save them, Idris,” I said. “I will save them. Years from now we will tell them about these fears, when both the fears and their cause have passed away. Even if they alone remain on earth, they will live. Their cheeks will not grow pale, nor will their sweet voices weaken.” Our eldest understood something of what was happening around him. Sometimes he would look at me gravely and ask why there was so much destruction. But he was only ten, and the natural happiness of youth soon cleared his face of worries beyond his years. Evelyn was a laughing little angel, a playful child who knew nothing of pain or sorrow. Tossing his fair curls out of his eyes, he made the halls ring with laughter and drew our attention to his games in a thousand innocent ways. Clara, our lovely, gentle Clara, was our support, our comfort, and our joy. She took it upon herself to nurse the sick, comfort the grieving, help the old, and join the games and encourage the happiness of the young. She moved through the rooms like a kindly spirit sent from heaven to brighten our dark hour with an unearthly light. Gratitude and praise followed wherever she went. Yet when she stood modestly before us, playing with our children or busily performing small kindnesses for Idris, we wondered how so much courage, wisdom, and energetic goodness could dwell in her lovely, innocent features and the soft notes of her moving voice.

Summer dragged by, for we believed that winter would at least slow the disease. The hope that it might disappear completely was too precious, too deeply felt to speak aloud. When anyone carelessly voiced that thought, the listeners burst into tears and passionate sobs, showing how great their fears were and how little hope they had.

When we was back on the raft and he counted his money, he found he’d gathered eighty-seven dollars and seventy-five cents. Besides that, he’d brought along a three-gallon jug of whisky he found under a wagon when he started home through the woods. The king said that, taking everything together, it beat any day he’d ever spent in the missionary business. There warn’t any question about it, he said: heathens weren’t worth a pinch beside pirates when you was working a camp-meeting.

The duke had reckoned he was doing mighty well till the king turned up, but afterward he didn’t feel quite so pleased. At that printing-office he’d set up and printed two small jobs for farmers—bills about horses—and pocketed four dollars for them. Then he’d brought in ten dollars’ worth of advertisements for the paper, offering to print them for four dollars if they paid beforehand, which they did. A year’s subscription cost two dollars, but he took three at fifty cents each, so long as they paid him ahead of time. They’d meant to pay in cordwood and onions like usual, but he told them he’d just bought the business and cut the price down as far as he could afford, and meant to conduct it for cash. He set up a little poem he’d made himself, straight out of his own head—three verses, rather sweet and mournful—called “Yes, crush, cold world, this breaking heart.” He left it standing in type, ready for the paper, and didn’t ask a cent for it. Altogether he’d collected nine dollars and a half, and said he’d put in a pretty fair day’s labor earning it.

Next he showed us another small thing he’d printed without charging, since it was for ourselves. There was a picture of a runaway slave carrying a bundle on a stick over his shoulder, with “$200 reward” beneath it. The words were all about Jim, describing him exactly. They said he’d escaped last winter from St. Jacques’ plantation, forty miles below New Orleans, and probably headed north. Anybody that caught him and returned him would get the reward and their expenses.

“Now,” the duke says, “once to-night’s over, we can travel by daylight whenever we please. If we see somebody approaching, we can bind Jim’s hands and feet with rope, put him in the wigwam, and produce this handbill. We’ll say we caught him farther up the river and couldn’t afford passage on a steamboat, so our friends let us have this little raft on credit, and we’re taking him down to collect the reward.

In truth, I felt no apprehension for her. She was what is called a capable woman, well able to conduct her affairs without my help. Indeed, I suspect she had always considered me an idle lad, a mere encumbrance, fit only for raising castles in the air, and was somewhat pleased to see me go. The night was dark when I took leave of her. With the three creditors who had caused me such vexation serving as my aides-de-camp, I conveyed the balloon, its car, and its equipment by an indirect route to the place where the remaining articles had been stored. Finding everything there untouched, I at once set about my business.

“It was April the first. As I have mentioned, the night was dark, without a single visible star, and occasional showers of fine rain made us exceedingly uncomfortable. My principal concern, however, was the balloon. Despite its protective coat of varnish, it was becoming somewhat weighed down with damp; the powder, too, might suffer damage. I accordingly kept my three importunate creditors busily employed, packing ice about the central cask and stirring the acid in the others. Nevertheless, they continually plagued me with questions about my purposes for this apparatus, and complained bitterly of the dreadful exertions I demanded. They could not imagine, they said, what benefit there could be in soaking themselves to the skin simply to assist at such frightful incantations. I grew anxious and labored with all my strength, for I honestly believe the fools thought I had made a bargain with the devil, and that my present undertaking was, in short, no honest business. I greatly feared, therefore, that they might desert me altogether. Yet I managed to soothe them by promising to settle every account in full as soon as this undertaking was concluded. Naturally, they interpreted these assurances in their own fashion, doubtless supposing that, whatever happened, a vast store of ready money would soon fall into my hands. So long as they received all I owed them, with a little extra for their assistance, I dare say they cared scarcely at all what might become of my soul or my body.

“After some four and a half hours, I judged the balloon to be inflated enough. I therefore secured the car to it and placed all my instruments inside, taking care to include the condensing apparatus, a plentiful supply of water, and a considerable stock of provisions, among them pemmican, which packs a great deal of nourishment into a relatively small space.
